newsitem.title: HUNGARY: FEATURE - Hungary's '56 uprising based on illusions.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Hungary's '56 uprising based on illusions.

text.p: The military commander of Hungary's failed 1956 uprising recalls the day Soviet troops fled in terror as a fiery mushroom cloud burst into the sky above his beleaguered base.
"It was like a miracle," Bela Kiraly, now 84, told Reuters. "The Russians ran away because they believed these devil Hungarians had an atomic bomb."
The "mushroom cloud", according to Kiraly, was of the Russians' own making. A Soviet missile had slammed into a Hungarian ammunition dump. The effect was instantaneous.
"The airplanes disappeared in half a second, the tanks in five minutes, the infantry in 10 minutes. We won the battle."
Kiraly's forces, encircled in the dying hours of the Hungarian rebellion, were free to escape.
Kiraly's cloud was one of many illusions surrounding Hungary's 1956 revolution.
Another was that the Kremlin, headed then by Nikita Khrushchev, might let Hungary leave the Soviet bloc.
Yet another was that the West, which had made countless propaganda broadcasts urging Hungary to throw off the yoke of communism, might intervene.

And still another notion, shared by few, was that Hungary might somehow fight off the Soviet military machine which withdrew from Budapest for about a week at the end of October but returned with crushing force on November 3 and 4.
All of the great hopes that Hungarians had during the brief uprising -- the biggest challenge to that date by any East bloc country to Soviet rule -- turned out to be illusions.

Research made public in periodicals and at a conference in Budapest sponsored by Hungary's 1956 Institute and the National Security Archive of Washington shows that the Hungarian uprising demonstrated how firmly the Cold War power lines were drawn, and how the uprising helped to harden those lines.

Notes taken during meetings of the Soviet presidium and released since the collapse of communism depict a leadership initially divided between those who favoured crushing the uprising and those who wanted to recognise a revolutionary government headed by Hungarian moderate Imre Nagy.

Nagy made a series of concessions during the 13 days of the uprising to non-communists in his government over neutrality and free elections, culminating in an outright withdrawal from the Warsaw Pact military alliance of communist countries.

Citing notes from the presidium, The Hungarian Quarterly says Khrushchev wanted the Soviet Union to avoid being seen as "imperialist". This label they wanted to reserve for Britain and France as they looked to military force to reverse Egypt's nationalisation of the Suez Canal.
"The British and French are just beginning to make trouble in Egypt," Khrushchev said. "Let us not end up in the same company." But Khrushchev eventually did just that.

The Soviet presidium's final decision was aided by a speech given in Dallas by then-U.S. Secretary of State John Foster Dulles who said the Americans would not view a Hungary liberated from the Soviet bloc as a potential ally.

"This was a message to the Russians, of course, this was something that was said to calm them down, to give as an assurance to the Soviets," said Csaba Bekes, a research associate at the 1956 Institute.

"Logically it means you (the Soviets) can let them go, we won't take them...but the history of this speech has become very defensive because the Russians interpreted this as meaning, "It's okay, they won't do anything'."
At the same time, the West, through its propaganda broadcast channels Radio Free Europe (RFE) and Radio Liberty (RL), was giving the Hungarian people quite the opposite impression.
A summary of a report prepared in 1956 by William Griffith, then in charge of the Hungarian department of RFE, and made public recently, said the radio had not violated its guidelines.

"But (Griffith's report) revealed that RFE broadcasts in several cases had implied that foreign aid would be forthcoming if the Hungarians succeeded in establishing a "central military command', appealed to the Hungarians to "continue to fight vigorously' and even gave specific tactical advice to rebels."
Bekes said the radios were crucial to any evaluation of 1956. The West was reluctant to acknowledge its role.

"My opinion is that they did directly contribute. The policy of the United States was a two-faced thing and many people in Hungary did not know that but expected something would be done after so much talk," Bekes said.

The cost in human terms of the uprising's failure is striking. The Russians installed Janos Kadar to replace Nagy and a period of Stalinist repression, which Hungary had endured previously in the late 1940s and early 1950s, resumed.

"All in all, the repression affected more than 100,000 people. Tens of thousands were interned, 35,000 were tried, some 25,000 to 26,000 were eventually imprisoned and 229 were executed," according to a report given in September at the Budapest conference on the uprising.

"The peak of reprisals was the trial of Imre Nagy and his colleagues, followed by his execution on 16 June 1958. The trial of the prime minister who had been coaxed out of his Yugoslav refuge was the last grand political trial of the Stalinist kind in east-central Europe."
Kiraly, who fled to Austria and on to New York where he became a professor of military history at the City University of New York, said the uprising was doomed to fail.
"There was a euphoria and even in myself I felt a slight hope that we could get away with it...But at the end of October when the Soviets began to invade we lost more and more hope.
"We didn't think we could hold out against the Russians, not for a moment. We never thought that we could win a war against the Russians, or that the West would come."
